introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - SECTION B: COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **a)** Write a story based on the proverb, 'The pen is mightier than the sword'.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: a land quarrel between two villages that is turning violent.
2. The aunt, a quiet teacher, discovers the truth in old records.
3. The decision to write rather than to confront.
4. The letter, the newspaper and the radio.
5. Peace is made without violence.
6. The proverb explained and the narrator's lesson.

**Model composition (544 words)**

When the rains were late that year, the villages of Mbah and Nkeng, which had shared the same stream for two hundred years, began to quarrel over the strip of fertile land along its banks. At first the quarrel consisted of angry words at the market. Then someone burnt a farmer's hut at night, and soon men on both sides were sharpening machetes in their compounds. I was fifteen years old, and I remember that the whole region seemed to be holding its breath.

My aunt, Miss Nchang, taught English at the government school in Nkeng. She was a small, quiet woman who always kept a pen behind her ear, and many people thought she was too gentle to be useful in a crisis. One evening I found her at the kitchen table, surrounded by old papers from the council office. "Where did you find these?" I asked. "In the records," she said calmly. "Nobody had ever bothered to read them."

For three nights she studied the documents. On the fourth, she announced that she had discovered the truth. The disputed land had been sold twice, many years earlier, by a council official who had taken money from the leaders of both villages and had given each a signed paper. Neither village had stolen anything; both had been cheated by the same man. The quarrel rested on a lie that had stayed hidden in a drawer.

"Then we must tell the chiefs," I said. My aunt shook her head. "The chiefs are angry and the young men are armed. If I stand in the square and talk, they will not listen. But everybody listens to the radio, and everybody respects what is written."

So she took her pen. She wrote a clear, calm letter that explained the facts, quoted the dates and enclosed copies of the two papers. She insulted nobody. She ended with a simple question: "Shall we shed blood for a land that both of us were deceived into claiming?" She sent the letter to the editor of the regional newspaper and to the community radio station.

The following Saturday, the presenter read the letter on air, and the newspaper printed it on its front page. In every bar, taxi and farm, people repeated the facts. The two chiefs, who had refused to meet, telephoned each other. A week later, they sat together under the great tree at the border, with the divisional officer between them, and read the papers aloud. The authorities opened an investigation, and the land was shared by both villages under a written agreement.

I watched the men who had carried machetes shake hands. No gun had fired, and no house had burnt. A letter had succeeded where threats could only have caused more suffering. That evening, my aunt simply put her pen behind her ear and went on correcting her pupils' exercise books.

I understood then the meaning of the proverb that the pen is mightier than the sword. The sword can wound, but it cannot persuade; it can destroy a house, but it cannot build trust. The pen, used with truth and patience, can open minds, expose injustice and make peace. Today, as a student of journalism, I carry that lesson with me wherever I write.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Telling a story where force solves the problem: the story must be 'based on' the proverb, so writing must visibly overcome violence.
